Article Title: From 2018 to 2022, a Georgia nonprofit employee stole $96,713 meant for abused and neglected children, spending it on Netflix, Six Flags, lingerie and a home theater before pleading guilty
Article Text:
O’Neal worked as a programme specialist for Court Appointed Special Advocates of Polk & Haralson, Inc

How the payments were made

Officials say funds were meant for children

Investigation and guilty plea

Jennifer O’Neal, a former employee of a Georgia nonprofit that supports abused and neglected children, pleaded guilty to stealing $96,713 from the organisation between 2018 and 2022, according to the US Department of Justice. She used the money for personal expenses, including Netflix, Six Flags, lingerie and home theatre equipment.O’Neal worked as a programme specialist for Court Appointed Special Advocates of Polk & Haralson, Inc., known as CASA of Polk & Haralson. The nonprofit recruits, trains and supports citizen volunteers who advocate for abused and neglected children in courts and in the community.As part of her job, O’Neal was responsible for processing payroll and expense reimbursements for staff and volunteers. According to information presented in court, she used that position to make repeated fraudulent payments from CASA's bank accounts to herself and others.The payments were made between 2018 and 2022 and were not for legitimate CASA expenses. Some were presented as mileage payments for court appearances or conferences, while others were described as reimbursements for restaurants, groceries, utilities and clothes for staff, volunteers or children.Investigators found that some of those expenses were actually for O’Neal’s personal use.According to the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Georgia, some of the mileage claims were inflated, while others were based on journeys that never took place. The expense reimbursements were also used to cover purchases and bills that had nothing to do with the nonprofit's work.O’Neal used CASA funds to pay her own power, water and sewage bills, as well as her cell phone bills. Other payments were used for expenses at a Six Flags amusement park and for a Netflix subscription.The stolen funds were also used to buy softball equipment and lingerie, according to the court information. In another instance, O’Neal issued payments that were described as being for office supplies. The money was instead used to buy home theatre equipment, which she installed at her home.The DOJ said the payments were made frequently over several years rather than as a single incident. In total, O’Neal took $96,713 from CASA of Polk & Haralson.US Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg said the money had been intended to support abused and neglected children. “O’Neal violated her company’s core values, stealing tens of thousands of dollars meant to support the most vulnerable members of our community- abused and neglected children,” Hertzberg said. He also thanked state and local law enforcement agencies that worked on the investigation.The FBI also described the theft as a repeated act. Mitchell Jackson, Supervisory Senior Resident Agent in the FBI Atlanta's Cartersville Office, said O’Neal had not taken the money because of a single, sudden decision. “This was not a one-time, spur of the moment decision. Jennifer O’Neal frequently and repeatedly stole from her company for her own personal gain,” Jackson said. He added that the FBI was committed to investigating criminal conduct of this kind.Chris Hosey, Director of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, said organisations working with vulnerable people depend on employees to maintain high standards of integrity.“Organizations that serve vulnerable individuals depend on their employees to uphold the highest standards of integrity. O’Neal violated that trust for her own personal gain, stealing funds intended to serve abused and neglected children,” Hosey said.He also said the Georgia Bureau of Investigation would continue working with local, state and federal partners to hold people accountable for abusing positions of trust.O’Neal, 63, of Cedartown, Georgia, pleaded guilty to a criminal information charging her with theft of federal programme funds. The plea was announced by the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Georgia on September 15.O’Neal's sentencing is scheduled for December 17, 2026, at 3 pm. The hearing will take place before United States District Judge William M. Ray, II.
Article Summary: Jennifer O’Neal worked as a programme specialist for Court Appointed Special Advocates of Polk & Haralson, Inc. She pleaded guilty to stealing $96,713 from the organisation between 2018 and 2022. She used the money for personal expenses, including Netflix, Six Flags, lingerie and home theatre equipment.

Article Title: Seoul built an architectural installation from mushrooms and agricultural waste; its walls were grown rather than constructed
Article Text:
Walls of Public Life. Image Credit: ANOMALIA

Seoul’s mycelium walls turn mushroom waste into architecture

Image Credit: ANOMALIA

The wall was grown through a low-energy process

What made the facade different from an ordinary wall

The project connected Mumbai, Bandung and Seoul

What could grown building materials offer future architecture

Seoul became the setting for an unique architectural experiment in 2025, where a public installation was made from mushroom mycelium and agricultural waste instead of conventional building materials. Named as Walls of Public Life, the project was created by Mumbai-based Anomalia for the 5th Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism. Its blocks were grown using fungal networks that bind crop waste together, turning discarded organic material into lightweight building components. The installation offered a different way of thinking about walls, showing how some future construction materials could be cultivated rather than manufactured.The Walls of Public Life installation was created for the first outdoor exhibition of the Seoul Biennale, held at Songhyeon Green Plaza. According to Anomalia’s project website, the studio was invited to create one of 24 Walls of Public Life for the 2025 event, curated by Thomas Heatherwick. The project explored what building facades could become if they were grown from mushroom mycelium rather than produced entirely through conventional industrial processes.The material at the centre of the installation was mycelium, the root-like network of fungi. Instead of treating agricultural waste as something to discard, the project used it as the main growing material. Crop waste was mixed with mycelium cultures, allowing the fungal network to spread through the organic material and naturally hold it together.This gave the waste a new purpose. Anomalia states that each block used 2.1 kilograms of crop waste while weighing about 1.5 kilograms. The resulting material could then be shaped into architectural components without relying on the energy-intensive processes normally associated with many conventional construction materials.The production method was relatively straightforward. Once the crop waste and mycelium cultures were combined, the mixture was placed into moulds. The fungal network grew through the material and acted as a natural binding system. The blocks were then dried and stabilised, producing the components used for the Seoul installation.Architecture Lab, in its report on Walls of Public Life, describes the installation as being made from MycoBlox and Biobo panels, which are mycelium-based materials combined with agricultural byproducts. The fungal networks bind the organic material as they grow, producing lightweight components with significant compressive strength.Anomalia’s own account gives the blocks a tested compressive capacity of up to 1.5 tons. That detail is important because the project was not simply about making an unusual surface from mushrooms. It was also an attempt to demonstrate that materials grown from biological processes could have practical qualities suitable for architectural use.The installation was designed to look and behave differently from the sealed surfaces commonly found on buildings. Its porous structure allowed air and light to pass through, while its uneven texture created a surface that could be experienced through touch as well as sight. MYCL , the Indonesian material company involved in the research and production, describes the installation as a breathable and interactive facade. Its account says the MycoBlox provided 3D modular blocks, while the square BIBO panels created another layer within the structure.Instead of functioning simply as a solid division between people and their surroundings, the installation was intended to create a more open relationship between the structure, visitors and the surrounding environment.The unique wall was also the result of work spread across three countries. According to Anomalia, the design was developed in Mumbai, India, while the materials were grown in Bandung, Indonesia, in collaboration with MYCL. The finished components were then transported to South Korea and assembled at Songhyeon Green Plaza in Seoul.MYCL similarly describes the project as a cross-border collaboration between architectural design and material research. Its production model avoided the idea that every part of a building material has to come from a conventional high-heat manufacturing facility.The collaboration also brought together different areas of expertise. Anomalia handled design and research, while MYCL worked on material research and production. The project was supported by the Seoul Metropolitan Government and P4G(Partnering for Green Growth and the Global Goals 2030).The Seoul installation presented mycelium materials as biodegradable and carbon negative. MYCL describes that the materials were designed to return to the earth at the end of their useful life.Another feature was the use of a modular wooden framework. MYCL notes that the framework allowed the installation to be disassembled, supporting a more circular approach to construction rather than treating the structure as something permanently fixed in place. Architecture Lab describes Walls of Public Life as a practical test of mycelium composite blocks in an outdoor public setting, where the material faced rain, storms, humidity and regular human interaction.
Article Summary: Walls of Public Life was created by Mumbai-based Anomalia for the 5th Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism. Its blocks were grown using fungal networks that bind crop waste together, turning discarded organic material into lightweight building components. The installation was designed to look and behave differently from the sealed surfaces commonly found on buildings.

Article Title: Nepalese security guard won UAE’s Dh30 million lottery jackpot; he plans to split the $8.2 million fortune with 4 friends
Article Text:
Representative Image of Tayab Khan and his friends joyfully celebrating a Dh30 million lottery win (AI Generated Image)

The syndicate had been playing together for 18 months

Each of the 5 friends will receive Dh6 million

Khan plans to build a home for his family in Nepal

A Mahindra Thar and Rolex are among his personal plans

The win came after the UAE Lottery changed its jackpot format

Tayab Khan, a 26-year-old Nepalese security guard working in Abu Dhabi's Ruwais Industrial Area, became the first winner of the UAE Lottery's new Dh30 million grand prize after matching all 7 winning numbers in a May 27, 2026 draw. Khan did not watch the draw and instead discovered the result through an email notification during the Eid Al Adha holiday. The Dh30 million jackpot, worth roughly $8.2 million, was not his alone. Khan had bought the ticket as part of a 5-member syndicate called Future Millionaires, meaning the prize will be divided equally among him and 4 friends, giving each member Dh6 million, or about $1.64 million. Khan has said he plans to leave his security job, build a home for his family in Nepal and learn more about investment and business opportunities, while allowing himself a few luxuries, including a Mahindra Thar and a Rolex watch. This remarkable win demonstrates how persistent collective effort among close friends can transform ordinary aspirations into extraordinary opportunities, ultimately strengthening both personal relationships and financial futures.Khan moved from Nepal's Gorkha district to the UAE about 4 years ago and has worked as a security guard in the Ruwais Industrial Area. He had been participating in the UAE Lottery regularly since its launch, which took place in December 2024, and continued playing with his friends despite not initially winning a major prize.The group pooled money to buy lottery tickets and called themselves Future Millionaires, a name Khan chose before their eventual win. After the jackpot, he said he changed the group's name to simply "Millionaires". Two of his fellow syndicate members, Sandeep BK and Shishir Paudel, joined Khan when he spoke about the win at the UAE Lottery's offices. The winning draw was held on Wednesday, May 27. Khan had selected all 7 winning numbers at random and was not watching the live broadcast when the results were announced. Instead, he received an email later that evening. He initially expected the message to relate to one of the smaller prizes he had won in previous draws. When he opened it and saw Dh30 million, he said his hands and legs began shaking and that he could not speak.The friends had regularly pooled their money to participate, with the winning ticket bought collectively. The Dh30 million jackpot will therefore be divided equally between all 5 members of the syndicate. That leaves each person with Dh6 million, equivalent to roughly $1.64 million. Khan described the money as an opportunity to provide greater financial security for his family and said the win could give his friends the freedom to take new opportunities in their own lives. The group had already experienced smaller lottery wins, which encouraged them to continue participating. Khan said there had been periods when it felt as though the jackpot might never come, but the friends continued to believe they could eventually win.Khan's first major priority is building a house for his family in Nepal. He has said that owning a good home for his parents and wider family was already one of his biggest goals, and the jackpot will allow him to build the kind of house he had previously hoped for. He also intends to leave his job as a security guard and explore entrepreneurship and investment. After working as an employee for 4 years, Khan said he now wants to learn more about investing and move towards a different stage of his working life. His plans extend beyond the immediate financial windfall. Khan has spoken about using the money to create greater security for his family, while also taking time to consider what he wants to do next rather than making every decision immediately after the win.While most of Khan's stated priorities involve his family and his future, he has also identified a couple of personal purchases he has wanted for years. He told Gulf News and Khaleej Times that a Mahindra Thar SUV and a Rolex watch are both on his wish list. The purchases sit alongside his plans to build a family home and explore investment and business opportunities. Khan has also said he has not yet settled on all of his long-term plans. For now, the immediate focus is on celebrating the win with the four friends who shared the ticket and on working out how to use the money responsibly.Khan's jackpot came shortly after the UAE Lottery changed its grand-prize structure. The lottery launched in December 2024 with a Dh100 million grand prize, but changed to a format offering a Dh30 million top prize on a twice-weekly schedule in April 2026. Khan's May 27 win was the first Dh30 million grand-prize victory under the new format. The Lucky Day draw uses a calendar-style format. Players select 6 numbers from 1 to 31 in the "day" section and 1 number from 1 to 12 in the "month" section, making 7 selections in total. Khan matched all 7 numbers in the May 27 draw. Participants must be UAE residents aged at least 18 and register through the lottery's official platform.Khan has also urged other players to approach the lottery responsibly. His message after the win was not simply to keep buying tickets, but to participate within limits and only spend money that would not interfere with everyday expenses. For Khan and his 4 friends, the Dh30 million jackpot has transformed a routine lottery syndicate into a shared fortune. Each of the 5 members now has Dh6 million, while Khan plans to use his share first to provide his family with a home before exploring the investment opportunities that could shape his next chapter.
Article Summary: Tayab Khan, 26, is the first winner of the UAE Lottery's new Dh30 million grand prize. Khan bought the ticket as part of a 5-member syndicate called Future Millionaires. Each of the 5 friends will receive Dh6 million, or about $1.64 million. Khan plans to build a home for his family in Nepal and learn more about investment and business opportunities.

Article Title: Long Island Sound water quality improves in 2026 report; Western Narrows earns its first passing grade since 2008
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Western Narrows earns its first passing grade since 2008

How the other open-water regions of the Sound fared

Image: Wikipedia

What's behind Long Island Sound's continued improvement

Why Save the Sound warns the gains remain fragile

Save the Sound released its 2026 Long Island Sound Report Card, showing that water quality improved or remained stable across all five open-water regions of the Sound. The biennial report, based on 2025 monitoring data and detailed on Save the Sound's own Report Card project page, grades the open Sound using four water quality indicators and 62 bay segments across 46 bays and harbours using five. The standout finding indicated the historically worst-performing region, the Western Narrows near New York City. They posted their first passing grade in nearly two decades. Here's how each region fared, and what's driving the improvement. It's a hopeful sign that decades of cleanup efforts, from upgraded sewage treatment to stormwater management, may finally be paying off for one of the region's most storied waterways.The Western Narrows, which includes the waters around New York City, received a D grade in the 2026 report, Fox Weather reports, marking the biggest improvement of any region and the first time it has received a passing grade since Save the Sound began grading the area in 2008. Every prior year, the Western Narrows had received an F. Save the Sound's own project page notes the organisation has long identified high nitrogen and nutrient levels as the biggest overall problem affecting the Sound's health, contributing to dead zones, algae blooms and marsh damage, particularly in this densely populated western stretch of the estuary.Beyond the Western Narrows, every other open-water region either improved or held steady. According to CT Mirror, the Western Basin improved from an A- to an A, and the Central Basin improved from an A to an A+. The Eastern Basin maintained its A+ grade, while the Eastern Narrows remained at a B. Altogether, the Western, Central and Eastern basins all received A grades in 2026. These open-water grades are based on four indicators, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll a, water clarity, and dissolved organic carbon. Meanwhile the bay grades draw on five indicators, including dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll a, water clarity, temperature, and the presence of seaweed.Save the Sound attributed the gains largely to billions of dollars in wastewater and infrastructure upgrades across Connecticut and New York, alongside continued reductions in the nitrogen entering the Sound. Excess nitrogen fuels algae blooms and contributes to low-oxygen conditions that can harm or kill fish and other aquatic life, so cutting nitrogen inputs has remained a central focus of the region's water quality efforts. Save the Sound's Unified Water Study has supported this work by establishing standardised monitoring procedures, protocols and equipment across 62 of the Sound's bays and harbours, allowing data collected by different organisations to be reliably compared region-wide.Despite the improving picture, Save the Sound via Fox Weather cautioned that this progress could still be undone. The organisation pointed to climate change, rising water temperatures and worsening stormwater runoff as ongoing threats to the Sound's recovery. Save the Sound said continued reductions in nitrogen pollution, along with sustained investment in wastewater and stormwater infrastructure, will be essential to maintaining the results achieved so far.
Article Summary: Save the Sound released its 2026 Long Island Sound Report Card, showing that water quality improved or remained stable across all five open-water regions of the Sound. The standout finding indicated the historically worst-performing region, the Western Narrows near New York City. Save the Sound attributed the gains largely to billions of dollars in wastewater and infrastructure upgrades across Connecticut and New York.

Article Title: How piles of elephant dung outside a Thai village became sun-cured bricks for the sculptural Goya Tower
Article Text:
Image: Spaceshift Studio

From roadside waste in elephant villages to a recognised sustainable building material

Left/Boonsem Premthada (Image: Spaceshift Studio)/Right/Goya Tower(Image: Boonserm Premthada)

Building Goya Tower brick by hand-shaped, sun-cured elephant dung brick

Why the tower is named after an elephant, and where it stands near Phang Nga's Elephant Mountain

Part of a longer-running elephant-dung design practice, not a one-off architectural stunt

In 2021, once the multi-year Elephant World project in northeastern Thailand was finished, architect Boonserm Premthada kept noticing the same thing on his return visits to the elephant villages, dung everywhere on the roads, outside houses, piled up around town as the local elephant population grew. "My approach to my practice doesn't come from theory; it comes from the soul," Premthada said via Azure, reflecting his instinct to treat the problem as material rather than waste. He began experimenting with the dung as a construction ingredient, mixing it with soil, cement, stucco, tree bark, leaves and plant-based pigments to form bricks.That early test, a single sample from Ta Klang Village, has since grown from small installations into a full building, Goya Tower, a sculptural structure now standing in Phang Nga, southern Thailand, built almost entirely from handmade elephant dung bricks. What began as a way to manage an overlooked byproduct has turned into a distinctive architectural language, one that turns a village's waste problem into its most visible landmark.Elephant dung is mostly partly digested grass, leaves and fruit, and it already serves as a raw material for products like paper, fertiliser and insect repellent, but turning it into a structural building component was new territory. Premthada's first public tests came at the Île-de-France Architecture and Landscape Biennial in 2022, and later at London's Academy of Art, where he worked with dung sourced from Colchester Zoo and local volunteers, proof, he found, that the method could travel to a different city and still work, since it depends on the place and scale of each project.He carried the same thinking into the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, where he built the Elephant Chapel, an archway formed from elephant dung discs, and into his broader philosophy of material use. Rather than framing the dung as "recycled" or "upcycled," he thinks in terms of a material's whole life cycle rather than only its afterlife, a distinction he treats as the real meaning of scaling up an idea.For the tower itself, workers shaped the dung into circular bricks 33 centimetres across and 5 centimetres thick, forming each one by hand and curing it with sunlight, human labour and time rather than industrial firing, a deliberately low-tech process that turned a waste stream sitting around the villages into a repeatable, modular building unit. The bricks come in five natural, sunset-inspired colours, arranged in a planned pattern. Builders threaded the individual bricks onto central steel rods and stacked them by colour into cylindrical columns of varying heights, so that the bricks function as both the tower's surface and its structural core. Together, the columns define the tower's curved internal walkways. Visitors can climb through the structure, and as they move upward, light and shadow guide them through changing views of the surrounding roads, gardens, forests and sea.The tower takes its name, Goya, from a local female elephant, and it stands as a public lookout at the entrance to Matalay, a large resort development in Phang Nga. According to Interesting Engineering, the site sits near Khao Chang, "Elephant Mountain," a limestone formation that resembles a reclining elephant and is tied to local legend. Elephants have shaped the region's forests, settlements and traditions for generations, and the tower, designed by Premthada with his firm Bangkok Project Studio, founded in 2003, is meant to make that relationship between animal, material and place visible.Goya Tower isn't an isolated gimmick; it's the latest, most public chapter in a design line Premthada has been developing since 2021 with pieces like the Elephant Theatre Pavilion and his Venice Biennale installations. His broader body of work, including the roughly 480,000-hand-fired-brick Elephant World museum in northeastern Thailand, has long centred on designing with elephants rather than only for the humans who live alongside them, an approach he describes as architecture that isn't human-centric. "I never intended to create something new. I only wanted to create something necessary," Premthada has said, describing his goal as something that lets people, elephants and the local economy keep circulating together. That underlying philosophy is what makes Goya Tower legible, a building material found by paying attention to what a community already has too much of, and a design system built to let visitors physically move through the result.
Article Summary: Goya Tower in Phang Nga, southern Thailand, is built from elephant dung bricks. The bricks are hand-shaped, sun-cured and cured by hand rather than fired. The tower takes its name, Goya, from a local female elephant and stands as a public lookout.

Article Title: An Italian town is rebuilding its school with 70% of the old building's demolition waste; it will also collect rainwater
Article Text:
PC: Wikipedia

What is being planned for the new primary school in Castel Madama

PC: Wikipedia

Around 70% of demolition waste will be reused or recycled

How will the new school save energy and resources

Inclusion across learning and community

An Italian town is replacing its existing primary school with a building designed to reuse the old structure’s demolition waste. The project in Castel Madama, called ‘New School: Innovation, Inclusion’, will reuse, recycle, or recover about 70% of the demolition waste from the existing school. According to the New European Bauhaus Prizes , it will collect rainwater and groundwater as part of the design.The school will include solar panels, high-performance insulation and natural materials with a low carbon footprint. It is designed as a Nearly Zero Energy Building (NZEB) and aims to use at least 20% less energy than NZEB standards. The building will have flexible learning spaces, green areas, and community facilities.The new primary school will replace the existing school on Via della Libertà, ‘O. VULPIANI’, in Castel Madama. The building follows New European Bauhaus principles of beauty, sustainability, and inclusion. Its design includes bright, flexible learning spaces for students and teachers, along with green areas and playgrounds.The building will also be safe and anti-seismic. Public areas will remain available outside school hours, allowing the site to serve purposes beyond regular lessons.The school is currently under construction and is expected to open in the 2026/27 school year. The project is intended to create a modern learning environment while also providing spaces that can be used by the wider community.The project takes a circular approach to the materials from the existing school. About 70% of demolition waste from the structure will be reused, recycled, or recovered. This will reduce the amount of material that needs to be discarded during construction.The project will also limit the amount of additional land used for the new building. Its footprint will expand by only 5% compared with the previous one. The approach is designed to retain green areas around the school while making use of the existing site.Along with the treatment of demolition waste, the project includes natural materials with a low carbon footprint. These choices form part of the wider design approach for the new school.Energy efficiency is another key part of the new school’s design. The building is planned as a Nearly Zero Energy Building, or NZEB, and aims to consume at least 20% less energy than NZEB standards.High-performance insulation will help support this target, while solar panels will provide renewable energy. The design also includes natural materials with a low carbon footprint. A rainwater and groundwater collection system will form part of the building’s resource management.Together, these features are intended to reduce the school’s energy and resource use. The project also includes a ‘green classroom’ for outdoor learning and environmental education, connecting the school’s design with its surrounding green spaces.The new building is designed to remain useful to the local community beyond school hours. Its public areas, green spaces and playgrounds will be available for cultural, educational and social activities. The design also focuses on accessibility, with ramps, elevators and clear signage to remove architectural barriers.Classrooms and common areas follow the design for all principles, while flexible and modular furniture can adapt to different needs. Students, parents and teachers have taken part in the design process. The Children’s Council also contributed to decisions about classroom layouts, green spaces, learning environments and furniture.
Article Summary: The new primary school will replace the existing school in Castel Madama, Italy. It will include solar panels, high-performance insulation and natural materials with a low carbon footprint. It is designed as a Nearly Zero Energy Building (NZEB) and aims to use at least 20% less energy than NZEB standards.

Article Title: Bangladesh to replace planned sculptures at historic sites
Article Text:
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman

DHAKA: The Tarique Rahman government has proposed replacing planned sculptures commemorating Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's March 7, 1971 speech and the surrender of Pak forces the same year with water fountains at Suhrawardy Udyan.The proposal is part of a plan to "rescope and repurpose" the Independence Monument project, according to sources at ministry of liberation war affairs.Originally known as Ramna Race Course, Suhrawardy Udyan is a national memorial and public space located in Dhaka. The site, covering an area of 95 acres, is notably associated with two pivotal moments in Bangladeshi history: the historic speech by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 7 March, 1971, calling for struggle against the Pakistani establishment and the surrender of Pakistani forces on 16 Dec, 1971, which marked the end of the Bangladesh War of Independence.The project, titled "Construction of the Independence Monument at Suhrawardy Udyan in Dhaka", began in 2018 and is scheduled for completion in June 2027. Its original design included sculptures at the two historic sites. Work had stalled since the change of govt in 2024.
Article Summary: The proposal is part of a plan to "rescope and repurpose" the Independence Monument project. Suhrawardy Udyan is a national memorial and public space located in Dhaka. The site is notably associated with two pivotal moments in Bangladeshi history.

Article Title: In 1888, George Vanderbilt began building a vast North Carolina estate; 26 years later, his widow sold 86,700 acres for $433,500, helping create the core of Pisgah National Forest in 1916
Article Text:
Building a cradle of forestry

Anchoring public land conservation

Enduring environmental heritage

A major property deal that began more than a century ago with a grieving widow turned a huge private wilderness in North Carolina into one of the most important public conservation achievements in American history. In May 1914, Edith Vanderbilt agreed to sell 86,700 acres of valuable mountain forest from the private Biltmore Estate to the United States federal government for $433,500. The deal was made at $5.00 per acre and moved the huge forest area into public ownership. The land later became the foundation of Pisgah National Forest, which was formally established in 1916. The sale carried out the conservation plan of her late husband, George Washington Vanderbilt. He began buying worn-out farmland and mountain slopes near Asheville, North Carolina, in 1888. Over 26 years, he collected more than 125,000 acres to build a self-sufficient mountain retreat centered around the 250-room Biltmore House.When George Vanderbilt first bought land in Western North Carolina, years of uncontrolled logging and burning had badly damaged local watersheds and forests. To restore the land, Vanderbilt hired famous landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted and young forestry expert Gifford Pinchot, who later became the first chief of the United States Forest Service.Under their direction, the Biltmore property became a testing ground for scientific forest management and soil restoration across the American South. In 1898, German forester Carl A. Schenck founded the Biltmore Forest School on the estate. It became the first school of professional forestry in North America. After George Vanderbilt unexpectedly died in March 1914 from complications following surgery, keeping the huge private property became a major financial burden for his widow. Edith Vanderbilt chose to follow her husband's wish to preserve the mountain wilderness instead of selling the land to commercial timber companies. According to historical records documented by the Forest History Society, Edith wrote directly to United States Secretary of Agriculture David F. Houston on 1 May 1914 to formally offer the land to the federal government. In her letter, she explained that she wanted the land protected for the public. She wrote: "I wish to sell this tract of land to the Government at a price significantly below its commercial value in order that my husband's plan for the protection of these mountain forests may be permanently realized."The purchase was made possible by the Weeks Act, a federal law passed by the US Congress in 1911. It allowed the federal government to buy private land in eastern states to protect the headwaters of navigable rivers and manage forest resources. The National Forest Reservation Commission, led by Secretary Houston, soon approved the deal. Official commission records in the Forest History Society archives show that the government viewed the $5-per-acre price as an exceptional bargain. Private timber companies had offered much more for the right to harvest the forests. The transaction was completed in 1914, leaving only 10,000 acres around the main Biltmore House and its immediate grounds in private family ownership. On October 17, 1916, President Woodrow Wilson issued an executive proclamation creating Pisgah National Forest, with the former Vanderbilt land forming its central area.The purchase protected important headwater areas for major river systems in the region, including the French Broad River basin. Today, Pisgah National Forest covers more than 500,000 acres across the Appalachian Mountains. Millions of people visit the forest each year for hiking, scientific research, and wildlife conservation. The birthplace of American forestry is still preserved within the forest at the Cradle of Forestry in America National Historic Site. The site stands on the same grounds where Schenck's students once attended their original field lectures. By accepting a much lower price for the land, Edith Vanderbilt protected both the financial future of the remaining estate and a large area of North American wilderness for future generations. The deal remains one of the largest single land purchases made under the Weeks Act and helped set an example for protecting public land across the eastern United States.
Article Summary: In May 1914, Edith Vanderbilt agreed to sell 86,700 acres of valuable mountain forest to the United States federal government for $433,500. The deal was made at $5.00 per acre and moved the huge forest area into public ownership. The land later became the foundation of Pisgah National Forest, which was formally established in 1916.

Article Title: Three siblings in Essex cut down their neighbours’ 33-foot Leylandii trees after a boundary row; the dispute ended with about £30,500 in damages and £178,668 in the neighbours’ legal costs
Article Text:
View from Robert McCarthy's home towards the old Leylandii trees at the bottom of the garden. (Photos: The Standard)

Dispute turns into court battle

Couple said they stopped using their garden

Foulla Bowler and John Barberis outside Central London County Court.

Judge orders damages and legal costs

£105,000 tree replacement rejected

Three siblings in Essex were ordered to pay about £30,500 in damages and £178,668 in their neighbours’ legal costs after cutting down a row of 33-foot Leylandii trees during a long-running boundary dispute. The court found that the siblings had trespassed into their neighbours’ garden and acted in a 'high-handed' and 'bullying' manner.According to The Standard, the dispute involved Robert McCarthy, 59, his wife Amanda, 61, and their neighbours Foulla Bowler, 61, John Barberis, 63, and Mary Englishby, 59. The McCarthys had lived in their home in Nazeing, Essex, since 2001, while Bowler had grown up in the neighbouring family home, which she now owns with her brother and sister.The two properties were separated by a fence, with a line of Leylandii trees on the McCarthys’ side. But around 2018, a dispute began over where the actual boundary between the gardens lay. Bowler and her siblings claimed the boundary was beyond the fence and that the trees therefore stood on their land.The disagreement eventually led to the removal of the fence and the cutting down of most of the trees in January 2022.The McCarthys said the loss of the trees left their garden exposed, damaged their privacy and changed how they used their home. They later took the siblings to court.The court heard that the McCarthys believed the old fence marked the boundary when they bought their home. Robert McCarthy said the trees were already well established at the time.“The trees were well-established when we moved in,” he told the judge, as quoted by The Standard. “We thought the chain link fence was the boundary as it ran along. I had no reason not to believe that to be the boundary,” McCarthy added.The siblings, however, maintained that the fence and trees were actually on their land. They said they had the right to remove them because they were causing 'overshadowing' and could potentially damage their property.The dispute continued for several years. Bowler had applied in 2018 for permission to fell 29 trees. According to the McCarthys’ barrister, Christopher Coyle, the family later went ahead with the removal, with the felling continuing into a second day even after the McCarthys’ lawyers had written to ask them to stop.Robert McCarthy described the work as an “invasion” and said it had resulted in a “relentless destruction of my garden. This is how we feel as a family. I can stand upstairs in my house and they can see me walking around. I want my privacy back like I had,” he told the court.The McCarthys told the court that the removal of the trees had affected their family’s everyday life. They said they no longer felt comfortable using the back garden and had stopped inviting people, including their children’s friends, to their home.Amanda McCarthy said they had “only ever used the front rooms of their house” since the trees were removed. She also told the court that she had become “depressed as a result of the stress that has been caused”.“After the invasion it feels completely destroyed. There's little or nothing left of what was our garden. Since the invasion we don't use the garden at all,” she said.The couple had sought compensation that included the cost of planting new trees and restoring their privacy. They also asked the court to declare that the true boundary was the line of the old fence.In an earlier judgment following a trial, Judge Alan Saggerson ruled in favour of the McCarthys on the location of the boundary. He found that the siblings had trespassed into the neighbours’ garden when they removed the trees.The judge said the siblings had taken “unilateral action to re-order the disputed boundary” during what he described as “fence wars” between the neighbours.He also said their evidence was less reliable and less accurate than that of the McCarthys. However, he did not find that the siblings were lying. Instead, he said they had “persuaded themselves of the righteousness of their own case.”At a further hearing this week, Judge Saggerson ordered the siblings to pay around £30,500 in damages and £178,668 towards the McCarthys’ legal costs. The amount comes on top of the siblings’ own court costs.The judge said the cutting down of the trees had caused a trespass and had a serious effect on the McCarthys’ use of their property.“The centre of gravity in this case is the cutting down of trees on or around the border, which in my judgment caused a trespass and had a serious impact on the claimants’ amenity in a number of ways. It opened up their rear garden to the unwanted attention of their neighbours,” he said.The judge also referred to “unfortunate acrimonious shouting and terms of abuse being hurled from the defendants’ garden into the claimants’ garden”. He said the couple had stopped inviting people round and that their children had particularly stopped inviting friends.“The loss of privacy was significant in a domestic situation such as this. From January 2022 I accept that the claimants had to live more and more, almost exclusively, at the front of their house,” he said.The judge further said the situation had a detrimental effect on Amanda McCarthy’s mental health. He also criticised the siblings’ “aggressive and somewhat bullying behaviour”. “It seems clear to me that the claimants have been victimised by high-handed oppressive behaviour. It goes way beyond the ordinary course of trespass,” he said.The McCarthys had sought enough money to replace the removed trees with new trees measuring about 8 metres tall. That work was estimated to cost £105,000.Judge Saggerson refused to award that amount. He said, “No reasonable person spending their own money would do this,” and instead awarded the couple £5,000 for smaller trees that could be planted and allowed to grow.The judge also noted that the siblings’ property was being marketed, or was expected to be marketed. Following the ruling, the three siblings are selling their childhood home, according to the court hearing.
Article Summary: Three siblings ordered to pay £30,500 in damages and £178,668 in legal costs after cutting down a row of Leylandii trees during a boundary dispute. The court found that the siblings had trespassed into their neighbours’ garden and acted in a 'high-handed' and 'bullying' manner. The dispute involved Robert McCarthy, 59, his wife Amanda, 61, and their neighbours Foulla Bowler, 61.

Article Title: A 14-year-old Georgia student scored a perfect 1600 on the SAT after taking college-level courses; Ashrit Talluri of Fulton County achieved the maximum score while still in an age group far younger th
Article Text:
A much earlier start to the SAT

He is already taking college courses

From test preparation to a future in medicine

A 14-year-old student in Georgia has achieved the highest possible score on the SAT, completing a test generally associated with students much further along in high school. Ashrit Talluri of Fulton County earned a perfect 1600 on the exam, according to FOX 5 Atlanta and The Independent, with additional reporting from outlets including Andhra Jyothy confirming his academic background and current studies. The SAT has a maximum score of 1600, made up of Reading and Writing and Math sections, each scored out of 800. College Board data places a 1600 in the 99+ percentile among its comparison groups.Talluri’s academic path had already moved beyond the usual pace before he sat for the exam. While in middle school, he completed 14½ high school credits. That coursework helped him qualify for college-level summer programs at Harvard and Rice.His father and middle school counselor encouraged him to take the SAT, and he registered in January. He then spent about five months preparing, working with a tutor, using online study material and completing more than two dozen practice tests. FOX 5 reported that he had already achieved a 1600 on three practice SATs before taking the official examination.Talluri eventually took the official test in June. The waiting period that followed was particularly significant because his result went through verification before being released.When the score arrived, it showed a perfect 1600.The achievement is notable partly because of Talluri’s age. College Board’s SAT percentile comparisons are based largely on students in grades 11 and 12 or recent graduating classes, while Talluri was only 14 when he took the exam.The SAT result is only one part of Talluri’s academic workload. He has now entered ninth grade at Fulton County’s Innovation Academy, where he is taking two college-level courses through dual enrollment. His interests also extend beyond conventional classroom work. Talluri participates in hackathons around the Atlanta area and is involved in chess and aviation. His public LinkedIn profile also lists interests and activities spanning artificial intelligence, medicine, computer science and research.Rather than leaving test preparation behind after achieving his own goal, Talluri has continued working with SAT material. He spends some of his free time creating practice questions and exploring strategies that could help other students prepare for the exam.Talluri has said he hopes to become a neurosurgeon, a career that aligns with his interest in both medicine and technology. His public professional profile describes him as a student interested in AI and medical applications, while also listing projects and extracurricular activities connected to those fields.His profile also identifies him as the founder of CerebroAegis, a project focused on using smartphone sensors for potential stroke screening and health-safety support. The project is presented as an AI-based health technology initiative rather than as a substitute for medical diagnosis.For now, however, Talluri is still a ninth-grade student balancing college-level coursework with extracurricular interests and academic competitions. His perfect SAT score may have come years earlier than expected, but his academic path is continuing to move forward. The next stage will involve the same combination of advanced coursework, technology interests and preparation that has already taken him well beyond the conventional school timeline.
Article Summary: Ashrit Talluri of Fulton County, Georgia, earned a perfect 1600 on the exam. The SAT has a maximum score of 1600, made up of Reading and Writing and Math sections, each scored out of 800. College Board data places a 1600 in the 99+ percentile among its comparison groups. While in middle school, he completed 14½ high school credits.

Article Title: Meet Erin Gardner, the Westford student raising $2,200 to rebuild a 24-foot trail bridge; she has already raised $1,125 and plans to replace its railings so children can safely keep using the path
Article Text:
A bridge that has connected the community for years

The project is also an Eagle Scout milestone

Her connection to the outdoors

A project backed by local support

A deteriorating trail bridge in Westford, Massachusetts, is at the centre of a student-led effort to preserve an important route used by children and families in the community. Westford Academy student Erin Gardner is raising $2,200 to restore a damaged section of the bridge as part of her Eagle Scout project, according to a September 24 report by The Westford Villager, published through WestfordCAT. Details on Gardner’s fundraising page confirm that the planned work includes rebuilding a 24-foot portion of the structure and replacing its railings.The bridge, known locally as the Academy Bridge, forms part of a network of wooded trails connecting Westford Academy with nearby schools and recreational areas. For years, the trails have offered students a way to move between the schools and surrounding sports fields without relying entirely on roads.Time, however, has taken a toll on the wooden structure. A 24-foot section has deteriorated to the point where part of it has fallen toward the water below, while the railings also require replacement.Rather than allowing the crossing to become unusable, Gardner has taken on the task of helping restore it. Her GoFundMe campaign sets a $2,200 fundraising target, with the money intended to support the materials and work required for the restoration.When The Westford Villager reported on the project on September 24, the campaign had collected $1,125.For Gardner, the bridge is not simply a community repair project. It is also part of her journey toward earning the rank of Eagle Scout, one of the highest achievements available in Scouting.The project gives her an opportunity to put the leadership and service skills she has developed through Scouting into practice while addressing something that has a direct impact on people around her. According to her fundraising page, the restoration will focus on replacing the damaged 24-foot portion and installing new railings along the bridge. Once completed, the work is expected to make the crossing usable for the community again.Gardner’s choice of project also reflects her wider involvement in outdoor activities. She is a member of Westford Academy’s Cirrus club, an organisation that encourages students to spend time outdoors and build connections through activities in nature.The group has organised hikes and overnight outdoor challenges, including trips to places such as Mount Monadnock. For students involved, these activities offer a break from the routines of school and an opportunity to spend time outdoors with friends.Gardner has previously spoken about the appeal of simply being outside, whether through hiking, climbing or informal activities with other students. That connection makes the bridge project particularly fitting. The structure is part of the same network of trails that allows students to experience the wooded landscape around their schools.Gardner’s Scouting journey has also earned recognition from people in the Westford community. Local resident Barbara Evangelista highlighted Gardner’s years of involvement in Scouts, including leadership responsibilities and participation in a 12-day Philmont trek, in a Facebook post referenced by The Westford Villager.The restoration campaign now brings those years of service into a project with a visible community purpose. Instead of creating something entirely new, Gardner is working to preserve a route that local students have already relied on for years.If the fundraising goal is reached, the damaged section and railings can be replaced, allowing the Academy Bridge to continue serving as a connection between the surrounding schools, trails and sports areas. For Gardner, reaching that goal would mean more than completing an Eagle Scout requirement. It would mean leaving behind a practical improvement that other children in Westford can continue to use long after her own school years are over.
Article Summary: Westford Academy student Erin Gardner is raising $2,200 to restore a damaged section of the bridge as part of her Eagle Scout project. The bridge, known locally as the Academy Bridge, forms part of a network of wooded trails connecting Westford Academy with nearby schools and recreational areas. A 24-foot section has deteriorated to the point where part of it has fallen toward the water below.

Article Title: In 1988, an 8-year-old tossed a bottle into the water off South Carolina; 29 years later, it was recovered on Georgia’s Sapelo Island and she got the note back
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing an 8-year-old girl releasing a handwritten message in a glass bottle into the Atlantic off Edisto Beach in 1988. Credits - Google Gemini

One hurricane in a bottle already lived through

Figuring out a stranger’s identity from 29 years ago

AI-generated representative image showing volunteers discovering a weathered message bottle on Sapelo Island after Hurricane Irma in 2017. Credits - Google Gemini

Why the note was more than the finding

Cleaning up after a hurricane is hardly anyone's idea of a fun afternoon, typically involving little more than carrying some trash off a beach and hoping the next storm is held up a little longer. For a couple cleaning up storm debris at Nanny Goat Beach, part of the Sapelo Island National Estuarine Research Reserve in Georgia, one afternoon in October 2017 became an afternoon unlike any they expected to have among the branches and garbage left behind by Hurricane Irma One of the pieces of wreckage was an ancient bottle, and in it was a note that had evidently been lying there for nearly three decades. According to reporting from ABC News affiliate WCIV, the note simply said, "Hello, my name is Miranda Dawn Moss. I am 8 years old and in third grade at Foster Park in Union, South Carolina. I came to Edisto Beach for a weekend." A small hand-drawn map came with the note, pinpointing the precise spot where the young girl and her family had slept on that long-ago weekend vacation.The note was dated September 1988, implying the bottle had been floating or sitting somewhere along the Southeastern coastline for 29 years before being discovered 90 miles from where it started.Miranda, 8, was visiting Edisto Beach with her family when she flung the bottle into the waves out of pure curiosity to see if it would ever wash up elsewhere, and if it did, whether anyone would bother writing back.She didn't have to wait long to doubt that it would be located. One year later, in September 1989, Hurricane Hugo , one of the most violent hurricanes to ever strike South Carolina, tore through that very stretch of coastline and Miranda herself assumed the bottle had been almost surely damaged or lost for good somewhere in the storm’s wake. Nothing for decades. The memory of a youthful whim had faded softly into that space where people forget they ever did something until something unexpectedly reminds them.The couple who found the bottle on Sapelo Island found it itself to be a bit of a puzzle: who was Miranda? They had just a maiden name, an age from 1988, and a location in South Carolina that might or might not have held anyone connected to her. Public records turned up a few phone numbers that led nowhere, and the pair eventually tried social media, uploading a picture of the handwritten note and asking anyone who knew the name or town to get in touch.That method performed far faster than the old-fashioned search had. Word spread from one connection to the next until it reached Miranda herself, married and far, far away from the third-grader who had stood on Edisto Beach with a bottle in her hand. Reconnecting after 29 years meant not just establishing that the note was indeed hers, but also filling in nearly three decades of two hurricanes, childhood memories, and the life events that had unfolded in the years after she let the bottle go.What made the eventual reunion so important wasn’t only the proof of the bottle’s provenance but also returning something that brought Miranda directly back to an 8-year-old version of herself she had mostly forgotten. The map she'd made, the neat handwriting, even the fact that she was in third grade, all of it preserved a certain, typical childhood moment that had somehow stayed perfectly intact over nearly three decades of tides, storms and shifting coastlines.Every few years, it seems, a story like this has surfaced along the Georgia and Carolina coastlines, each one with its own little twist but the same basic shape, a piece of somebody's past coming to the surface decades later, generally precisely when they've long since stopped expecting it. For Miranda, the return of that note wasn’t so much about the bottle, but rather about being given proof that some passing childhood wish, uttered on a beach weekend she probably would have forgotten entirely, had actually gone somewhere and mattered to someone, even if it took 29 years and two hurricanes for the message to finally arrive.
Article Summary: Miranda Dawn Moss was 8 years old when she threw a message bottle into the Atlantic off Edisto Beach, South Carolina in 1988. The bottle washed up on Sapelo Island, Georgia, in October 2017. A couple cleaning the beach found the bottle and a note that had been left in it. The note was dated September 1988, implying the bottle had been floating or sitting somewhere along the Southeastern coastline for 29 years before being discovered.

Article Title: In 1981, a Florida vacationer threw a message bottle into the sea; 36 years later, it washed up on a Georgia island and brought back a college memory
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a young vacationer releasing a handwritten message in a glass bottle into the Atlantic in 1981. Credits - Google gemini

The letter that had waited 36 years

Running across a stranger at an old address

AI-generated representative image showing a decades-old message bottle discovered on the shore of Little St. Simons Island, Georgia. Credits - Google Gemini

A statement that survived

Beachcombing seldom yields anything more thrilling than an odd shell or a piece of sea glass, which is part of the reason why some types of discoveries continue to halt people's progress decades after they occur. A peaceful barrier island off the coast of Georgia, Little St. Simons Island is the kind of spot where tourists spend their days searching for precisely that kind of little, ordinary treasure, meandering along the shoreline with no hope of discovering anything more than a lovely shell to take home.The note was short and rather formal for something designed to drift at random across the ocean. The bottle was let adrift off Fernandina Beach, Florida, on June 10, 1981, and it kindly urged anyone who found it to write back and tell where, when, and by whom it had been located. Doug Stephens was a twenty-year-old college student home on holiday from university who had signed the note, with his permanent address on the reverse, never figuring anyone would actually do anything about it decades later.It is that length of time that gives the story its resonance. Bottles thrown into the sea seldom find their way back to anyone, and those that do usually turn up within a few years, not decades. Ryan Burchett, the Georgia man who had picked the bottle out of the sand while beachcombing on Little St.Simons Island, eventually tracked down Stephens, now in his late fifties and living in another part of Georgia, having long ago given up hope of any response to a message he’d flung into the ocean on a whim as a young man vacationing with his family.Finding Stephens was a modest expedition in itself. The address on the note was hopelessly out of date, so Burchett turned to a local outfitting shop for help, which used social media to hunt down someone matching the specifications in the note. In the rather brief period of looking, they came into contact with Stephens personally, and the two men spent time on the phone, sharing memories of the precise stretch of Georgia and Florida shoreline where they’d both spent parts of their earlier years, separately.It was less about the bottle itself and more about what came after, the odd bridge it created between two strangers divided by an entire generation. As it happened, Stephens still came close to Burchett's hometown every year, en route to the same Florida beach where he'd thrown the bottle. The coincidence made the eventual reunion seem less random than it might otherwise have been. The two decided to meet in person so Burchett could return the bottle himself, and what started as a surprising find became more like an old friendship rediscovered after nearly four decades.Part of what makes this story land is simply how much had changed between the bottle setting out and finally arriving. It was cast into the water the same summer MTV first hit the airwaves, and it resurfaced in an age of smartphones and social media, tools that ultimately made tracking down its sender possible in a way that would have been unthinkable back in 1981. What sounds unusual is not actually rare in oceanographic terms. According to NOAA , a small drift card the agency released off the American east coast in 1977 spent 26 years circling the North Atlantic before finally washing ashore on a beach in Ireland, a reminder that objects can drift undetected for far longer than most people would guess.Both men, having lived through the experience firsthand, were quick to note that this particular form of communication belongs firmly in the past, pointing out that plastic and glass thrown into the ocean tend to linger indefinitely rather than delivering a tidy, sentimental ending. Even so, for two people who had never met before that summer, the bottle did exactly what it was designed to do all those years ago. It found someone, it carried a message across a gap of 36 years without losing a word, and it gave a college student's passing whim on a Florida beach an ending neither he nor its eventual finder could have predicted.
Article Summary: A glass message bottle was thrown into the Atlantic by a college student in 1981. The note urged anyone who found it to write back and tell where, when, and by whom it had been located. Ryan Burchett, the Georgia man who had picked the bottle out of the sand while beachcombing on Little St. Simons Island, eventually tracked down Doug Stephens, now in his late fifties.

Article Title: In 1924, Kansas City sealed a time capsule high inside its war memorial; 100 years later, crews drilled through concrete to uncover a president’s letter and century-old documents
Article Text:
AI Representation: Kansas City sealed a time capsule high inside its war memorial. Image credits: ChatGPT

How workers reached a box sealed since 1924

Aerial photo of the National WWI Museum and Memorial with the Kansas City skyline. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

What was found inside the copper box

Kansas City Star

Why the memorial itself carries lasting historical weight

What the reopened capsule means for the memorial's next century

In the early 1920s, Kansas City residents rallied behind an ambitious plan to honor the men and women who had served in World War I. The Liberty Memorial Association, formed by a group of prominent local citizens, raised more than 2.5 million dollars in just ten days in 1919, a sum equivalent to roughly 45 million dollars today, to fund construction of a towering monument south of Union Station. Ground was broken in November 1921 in a ceremony attended by five Allied military commanders and an estimated 100,000 spectators, and three years later, as the tower's stonework was going up, a copper box was sealed into its cornerstone with instructions that it not be opened for a full century.The box remained untouched through the memorial's public dedication in November 1926, when President Calvin Coolidge addressed a crowd of over 150,000 people. It stayed sealed through the decades that followed, even as the structure neared collapse and later underwent major renovations at the turn of the twenty-first century. The box was unearthed in the summer of 2024, when workers for the National WWI Museum and Memorial drilled into eighteen inches of limestone and concrete to recover it, one hundred years after its initial placement.Removal of the capsule turned out to be much harder than cutting into the wall.Workers had to saw through layers of limestone and concrete that formed the cornerstone of the tower, and their work became even more difficult after it was discovered that there was probably old nitrate film stored in the box, a material that decomposes unpredictably and can become highly unstable and prone to spontaneous combustion as it breaks down. For this reason, the bomb squad from the Kansas City Police Department came to check out the capsule before it was opened.As the National WWI Museum and Memorial explains on its own site describing the 1924 Time Capsule Unveiling , the original cornerstone ceremony had been a spectacle in its own right, with airplanes circling overhead, a band playing patriotic music, doves released into the air and remarks read aloud by the Allied commanders and President Coolidge. After ensuring that there were no safety issues involved, the museum revealed the contents of the capsule in an official ceremony held on October 16, 2024. The museum’s president and CEO, Matthew Naylor, delivered the relics to the audience, explaining that this was an attempt by the people of Kansas City to make sure that some part of them lived on in future generations.There were fifteen objects in total contained in the capsule, spread across several categories of documents and letters. Twelve had been reviewed and protected before the opening, and the other three were reviewed during the ceremony itself. Among them was a letter from President Coolidge to the Liberty Memorial Association in which he stated his delight in hearing that the association would be able to lay the foundation stone of the monument very soon, and a tube containing congratulatory letters of the Allied commanders who attended the groundbreaking ceremony of 1921. The capsule also held a copy of the U.S. Constitution and the American Declaration of War from April 1917, along with a Bible, newspapers from the period, the printing plate of thefrom November 1921, and magazines from the Kansas City Chamber of Commerce describing the city in the 1920s.The Liberty Memorial's significance extends well beyond the time capsule buried inside it. In 2006, the National Park Service designated the memorial a National Historic Landmark, a distinction reserved for properties judged to hold exceptional value in illustrating American history. According to the National Historic Landmark Nomination , the Liberty Memorial, built between 1923 and 1938, embodies the Beaux-Arts Classicism style that was the preference of architects of the time during the City Beautiful era of early twentieth-century America. This monument's size and symbolism demonstrate how significant World War I was to the civic consciousness of Americans in the years following. It is this same importance that made the sealed cornerstone valuable enough to protect for one hundred years, rather than just preserving the records inside the archives.Since the contents of the 1924 capsule are all accounted for, work has already commenced at the museum on planning the next steps. The museum officials have declared that in 2026, there will be another time capsule assembled and buried in celebration of the hundredth year of the monument being dedicated to the community. This cycle of burying and unearthing time capsules that began as an initiative by one organization to honor the sacrifice of one war has turned into an ongoing cycle of memory in itself, from one generation to the next in Kansas City.
Article Summary: Kansas City sealed a time capsule high inside its war memorial. The box was unearthed in the summer of 2024, when workers for the National WWI Museum and Memorial drilled into eighteen inches of limestone and concrete to recover it. The capsule held a copy of the U.S. Constitution and the American Declaration of War from April 1917, along with a Bible.

Article Title: In 1933, a secret giver mailed $5 checks to struggling families; 75 years later, his grandson opened an attic suitcase holding thank-you letters
Article Text:
AI Representation: A long-hidden collection of thank-you letters preserves the story of a secret giver’s generosity decades later. Image credits: Chatgpt

How the suitcase came to hold a stranger's secret

Why the discovery reached far beyond one family's attic

A Secret Gift

An old suitcase. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

What one suitcase revealed about a hidden act of generosity

In December 1933, at the depth of the Great Depression, a small advertisement appeared in the Canton Repository, a local newspaper in Canton, Ohio. Titled "In Consideration of the White Collar Man!", it was signed only by "B. Virdot" and promised financial help to families willing to write in and describe their hardship. The anonymous donor was Canton business owner Samuel J. Stone, who owned a menswear shop with his wife, Minna, and originally intended to send each of the seventy-five families ten dollars. So many letters of desperation arrived that he changed his mind and ended up giving five dollars to each of 150 families. He sent each of these donations via checks written at the same local bank and signed using the fake name he had created using the first names of all three of his daughters, Barbara, Virginia and Dorothy. The identity of Stone was kept anonymous and his secret remained hidden for seventy-five years until its revelation in June 2008. The secret was revealed by his grandson, writer Ted Gup, when he visited his mother for her eightieth birthday and took home with him an old suitcase filled with documents she thought he might be interested in looking at. He did not open the suitcase for months, but when he did, he found a bunch of tattered letters and bank statements dated December 1933.A review of the resulting book, published in a University of Minnesota library journal , describes how Gup pieced the mystery together only after finding the original Canton Repository clipping among the suitcase's contents, which named an anonymous donor signing as B. Virdot. A conversation with his mother verified through the paperwork that his grandfather had advertised and was sending five-dollar checks anonymously to families in the community who were suffering from the economic hardships of the Depression. It is mentioned in the review that while Sam and Minna Stone were not rich by today's standards, in the year 1933 they were prosperous enough to be able to run their own business, feed their children and have little luxuries when compared to many of their neighbors. In between the appeals for help were the checks themselves, cancelled and returned to Stone's own account after the families had cashed them, still bearing the signature of B. Virdot, along with thank-you letters from families to whom the money had been sent and who wanted to let this stranger know how much the help had meant to them.Moreover, according to the University of Minnesota review, as Gup delved deeper into the history of the items in the case, he was led into the exploration of his grandfather's whole life story, discovering the truth that Sam Stone was not originally from America but was from Romania, where he was known as Samuel Finkelstein. The book that resulted, titled, was later selected for the State Library of Ohio's Choose to Read Ohio program , which encourages public libraries and schools across the state to build community readership around Ohio authors. In the materials from that program, there is a record that after the story about Stone's secret generosity became known, the same idea was revived locally when community members modified the original $5 gift according to inflation rates to $100, and once again invited the Canton families to write in with their stories about their needs, repeating the exact thing that Stone had done secretly in 1933.In addition, the University of Minnesota review emphasizes the fact that the letters found in the suitcase revealed not only material difficulties. There were letters from some of the recipients explaining that they were keeping children from needy families because those families could not afford to provide for them, or postponing their layoffs in order to keep the business running as long as possible.The importance of the story does not lie in how much was at stake, but rather in the fact that Stone had never taken any of the credit for it all. He invented an entire new identity, just to make sure that those whom he helped could never give him the recognition he deserved. In order to find out who had helped his family, Gup had to discover a forgotten suitcase that had belonged to Stone's own family. For Gup, opening the suitcase was about more than solving the mystery within his own family; it was also about bringing to light the actions of a mysterious man who had quietly helped so many of his struggling neighbors during their toughest winter.
Article Summary: Samuel J. Stone sent five-dollar checks anonymously to families in Canton, Ohio. The identity of Stone was kept anonymous for seventy-five years. The secret was revealed by his grandson, writer Ted Gup, when he visited his mother.

Article Title: In 1998, an Ontario fourth-grader dropped a note into Lake St. Clair; 26 years later, it turned up in her daughter’s fourth-grade class at the same school
Article Text:
AI Representation: A decades-old message in a bottle makes an extraordinary return to the same school where it was first sent. Image credits: Chatgpt

How the bottle resurfaced after nearly three decades

Why a bottle could stay near the same shoreline for 26 years

Lake St. Clair Physical and Hydraulic Characteristics

Visualization of a Drifting Buoy Deployment on Lake St. Clair

Why the letter landed in her daughter's classroom

What the reunion meant for the family that wrote it

Shoreline muck in Lake St. Clair. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

In 1998, a fourth grader named Makenzie Morris typed out a letter about the waters of the Great Lakes on a computer in her classroom, as part of a class assignment from her teacher, Roland St. Pierre, at St. John the Baptist Catholic Elementary School in Belle River, Ontario. Once the letter was printed, nine-year-old Makenzie rolled it up, sealed it inside a plastic bottle with wax, and walked with her classmates to a pier where the Belle River empties into Lake St. Clair. There, roughly 32 students let their bottles go into the water, most likely never expecting to hear from them again. Twenty-six years later, in the fall of 2024, one of those bottles surfaced near the pier on the same lake where it had been thrown in. It was found by a kindergartner from the very same school, and it eventually made its way into a fourth-grade classroom where Makenzie's own daughter, now a student there herself, happened to be sitting.River Vandenberg, a St. John the Baptist student, found the bottle along the sandbar of Belle River pier in Lake St. Clair when he went exploring with his grandmother, Michele.As per Good Morning America, the rolled-up letter within was written by Makenzie Morris, now known by her married name Van Eyk, a nine-year-old student of Roland St. Pierre's fourth-grade class at the time. In fact, the letter contained instructions for whoever would find it to contact the school. Michele thought the letter could be part of some school activity and contacted the school directly without considering that it may be just trash. Her guess proved right very quickly. The teacher at the school responded immediately and informed them that the letter dated back to 1998, 26 years earlier. As per CBC News, St. Pierre, who is now retired, recalled that he had assigned the "message in a bottle" project to his class in 1998, and that only two other bottles from that group have since turned up: one appeared weeks later in Tecumseh, which is located 10 miles away from Belle River, while the other one appeared a year after that in Lake Erie, an outlier that the local wind-driven currents described below don't fully explain.Lake St. Clair's own physical characteristics help explain why a sealed bottle might resurface so close to where it was originally thrown in rather than drifting far away. A technical report from NOAA's Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory , discusses how the lake is described as having a shallow bottom whose surface currents are determined mainly by wind direction, not by strong currents. Since the lake lies between the inflowing St. Clair River and the outflowing Detroit River, it would make sense for the water movements to be influenced by winds and not just flow in one direction towards the river, thus giving anything floating a chance to get back into place instead of being washed away completely.A separate field study from the US Geological Survey adds more direct evidence of this behavior. In, researchers deployed twelve drifting buoys in the lake for 74 hours in August 2002 to analyze the circulation patterns of the lake as part of a water intake safety evaluation project. It was determined by the aforementioned researchers that the movement of the buoys depended largely on the prevailing winds at the time, such that the buoys would not always move in a direct line towards the outflow point but sometimes even in loops and sometimes backwards instead. Such erratic movement due to the wind is characteristic of a closed bottle that stays within the same general vicinity of shore for many years.River took the bottle to school, where a teacher from the fourth-grade class read the letter to the other children, an event which would turn out to involve Makenzie's own daughter, Scarlet Van Eyk. According to Smithsonian Magazine, Scarlet was present when the letter was read and recognized her mother's maiden name in it right away. Scarlet told CBC News that her jaw just dropped, and that as soon as classmates began asking her who had written the letter, she had to tell them that her own mother had written it. But that wasn't all. Scarlet is now a fourth-grader at St. John the Baptist, in the same class as her mother was in when she wrote the letter, so both mother and daughter reached this same milestone in the same grade, at the same school. St. Pierre also pointed out another coincidence, stating that he used to teach River's father, thereby linking this family to the small school community.Van Eyk mentioned that she never gave much thought to the bottle during the last twenty-six years, although she did sometimes wonder about its fate after she had thrown it into the water when she herself was just a child.
